heard: In 1850, the deadliest disease in the world  was also the most fashionable.  Pale skin, a thin waist, bright eyes, and pink cheeks.  People called it the look of consumption.
Lord Byron said he'd like to die of it, so the ladies would say how interesting he looks  in dying.
Darling, everyone who's anyone has me.
Today, you're a 20-year-old clerk in London, 1850.  You've just caught it.  Let's see the next three years.
Here's how you caught it.  Someone in your crowded office coughs.  Tiny droplets hang in the air for hours.  You breathe in a few bacteria, and that's enough.
Your immune cells swallow them, but they can't kill them,  so your body builds a prison around them,  a small hard lump in your lung.
In 1850 London, most adults have one of these prisons.  For most of them, the prisoner never gets out.
I'm very patient.
but you're overworked, underfed,  and you sleep in a cold, damp room.  The prisoner breaks out.
Month one. A cough that won't go away. You're tired all the time and a little thinner.  In the mirror you look fine, just tired.
Your handkerchief is still clean.
Inside, the bacteria are multiplying, eating into the soft tissue around the prison.
Your doctor's prescription is new and very modern.  Cod liver oil, a spoonful three times a day.  It tastes terrible.  And to be fair, it might actually help a little.
Month 6 Every afternoon a fever comes, two bright pink  spots burn on your cheeks, doctors called it the hectic flush.
At night, you sweat so much you wake up in soaked sheets.  You've lost your appetite and your collar is getting loose.
And one morning, there's a pink speck on your handkerchief.
Your doctor says your blood is too rich,  so he puts leeches on your chest.
Leeches. Lovely. Take more blood. I'll wait.
Year one, you cough and your mouth fills with bright red blood.
Here's why, the bacteria have eaten a hole right through your lung and broken a blood  vessel on the way.
And now, every time you cough, you spray bacteria into the room.  Your landlady's little boy has started coughing too.
The strangest symptom is in your head.  You feel hopeful, full of plans.  Doctors called it spes tisica, the hope of the consumptive.  Nobody knows why.
Your doctor's advice goes south to the warm air of Madeira or Italy.  On a Clark's wages, that's like being told to go to the moon.
Year two, in the mirror, a stranger.  Gray skin, hollow cheeks, huge shining eyes.  Your coat hangs on you like on a coat hook.
You're short of breath on the stairs.  Your voice has turned to a whisper.
Inside, both lungs are full of holes.
Now there are three ways this can go.
Path one, galloping consumption.  It speeds up and it's over in weeks.  About half of untreated people were dead within a few years.
Path 2. You drag on for years, half alive, coughing the disease into everyone around you.
Path 3. Your body builds new walls around the holes and the disease goes quiet. Some people  really did recover, with scars in their lungs for life.
I'll take any of the three.
Today, the same cough, three weeks long.  A doctor sends you for a chest x-ray  and a test of what you cough up.
The treatment is four drugs every day for six months.  You feel better in weeks, but you have to finish it  or the bacteria learn to resist.
And yet, tuberculosis still kills more than a million people every year, mostly where the  medicine is too far away.
Still here darling, still in fashion.
So, which path would you have got in 1850? Tell me in the comments.
